newsitem.title: UK: Guilt-free indulgence is good for you-scientists.
newsitem.headline: Guilt-free indulgence is good for you-scientists.

text.p: That sneaked cigarette or furtive glass of wine could do you the world of good if only health freaks weren't making you feel so guilty about it, British scientists said on Thursday.
A survey carried out in eight countries found that people around the world are plagued with guilt about the small pleasures in life.

This doesn't stop people indulging in alcohol, cigarettes and high-fat foods, but it does stop them from enjoying them, Associates for Research Into the Science of Enjoyment (ARISE) said, releasing the results of their survey.
The survey questioned 4,000 people about their attitudes towards a list of indulgences including smoking, eating chocolate and cakes, drinking alcohol and failing to exercise.
It found Australians are the world's most guilt-ridden people, while the Dutch were the greatest pleasure-takers and also least remorseful about their indulgences.

Only 13 percent of Dutch people felt guilty about their pleasures, compared with 27 percent of Australians and way ahead of the next most guilt-free nation, Belgium, where 19 percent of people said they anguished over their gratification.
Germans were least likely to take enjoyment from corporeal pleasures and also came second in the guilt league.
But scientists said moderate indulgence reduces stress, a benefit that can be completely outweighed by feelings of guilt.

"A favourite treat, such as a cup of tea or coffee, a glass of wine or beer, a cigarette or a bar of chocolate reduces stress and helps people relax," said Dr Neil Sherwood of the University of Reading in southern England.

"When people get caught in the guilt trap...they either try to sacrifice their enjoyment or live with the guilt. This can undermine the positive benefits of enjoyment which studies show can protect against stress and strengthen the immune system."
At its worst, stress can lead to depression and physical ailments such as heart disease and ulcers, he said.

The survey showed that 43 percent of Europeans said they would enjoy their pleasures more if they didn't feel so remorseful about indulging, suggesting that they weren't getting the stress-reducing benefits, according to ARISE.
"People should not feel guilty about pleasure-giving activities, as long as they don't over-indulge or harm others," said Professor David Warburton of ARISE.
